newsitem.title: CHINA: China market regulators go global with stock moves.
newsitem.headline: China market regulators go global with stock moves.

text.p: China's regulatory authorities have gone global by seeking to tighten control over asset injections into Chinese-controlled firms abroad, building on recent moves to police their own domestic share markets, analysts said on Sunday.

China's State Council, or cabinet, on Friday announced that the transfer of domestic assets into Chinese-controlled firms overseas would require government approval if the purpose was to inject the assets into a listed vehicle.
Analysts said the move was aimed largely at Hong Kong's "red chips" -- many of which have soared sky-high on investor expectations of valuable asset injections by Chinese parent companies.
Red chips are Hong Kong-based companies with financial backing from China.

"They (Chinese authorities) just want to make sure that there is no transfer of assets from mainland China to Hong Kong and an outflow of these types of assets," said Alex Tang, head of research at Yamaichi International in Hong Kong.
"They don't mind it (assets) going out as long as it is still under the control of the Chinese and they don't want to see an undervaluation of their assets," he said.

Red chips have risen meteorically since earlier this year on investors' appetite for speculative China plays and expectations that Beijing would want buoyant stock markets through the handover of Hong Kong to Chinese rule on July 1.
Similar beliefs about the handover had also caused China's domestic currency A shares to rocket until May, when market regulators launched moves to crack down on speculation.

"What's happened has to do with the government's crackdown on A shares," said another analyst at a Japanese securities firm in Hong Kong. "China wants to give the image that they run a serious market and not a casino."

China has barred listed firms, state enterprises and state banks from speculating on the domestic stock markets and the speculative nature of red chip trading -- in part fuelled by money from mainland China -- had caused alarm bells to ring in Beijing.

"In part, it's the same thing as the A share market," said an analyst at a European securities firm in Shanghai. "The government was worried the situation (with red chips) was getting out of hand and the market was going to crash."
The companies themselves were also ramping up their own values by swapping assets back and forth, analysts said.

"They (Chinese authorities) are trying to get more of the money away from the trading and speculative side and put it into projects such as infrastructure rather than just shifting assets from one vehicle to another and inflating the value without the usefulness of the asset," said Kent Rossiter, institutional sales manager at Nikko Securities in Hong Kong.

Hong Kong investors had expected the moves following recent rumours. The announcement did not appear aimed at damaging market sentiment or deflating the Hang Seng Index before the handover, analysts said.

Beijing is still learning to regulate its own stock markets and the foray into Hong Kong, which becomes part of China in just nine days, is an important step to convince the world it can manage its financial affairs, they said.
The State Council also announced that Chinese-controlled companies making share offers abroad must first obtain approval from domestic regulators.
It urged foreign stock offers to be made as direct listings, unlike some recent indirect stock sales that had sidestepped Beijing's market regulators.
The body also repeated a previous ban on the purchase of shell companies for the purpose of obtaining a foreign listing.
